claim.text: MesoNet, , achieves 56.2% test accuracy at 80% sparsity on the OpenForensic dataset, using approximately 3,000 parameters
At 80% sparsity on the OpenForensic dataset, MesoNet's 56.2% test accuracy corresponds to 89.8% of the dense MesoNet model's baseline accuracy (62.6%).
A highly compressed MesoNet subnetwork preserves most of the original detection performance on the OpenForensic dataset.

For CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic dataset, Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with global thresholds yields 80%-sparsity test accuracies of 90.88% , 94.29% , and 96.11% , respectively.
At 80% sparsity on the OpenForensic dataset, the CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet architectures contain sparse subnetworks that preserve almost all original performance.

For the FaceForensics++ dataset (a dataset of 11,600 training images from face-cropped frames of 400 videos with varied compression and deepfake generation artifacts), ResNet-18 pruned with Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) using local (per-layer) thresholds (20% weight removal per iteration for 8 rounds, Adam lr=$1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10) retains 83% test accuracy at 80% sparsity, outperforming both its dense baseline and the same network pruned using global thresholds. Thus, local pruning yields superior preservation of critical layer-specific features on compressed, challenging datasets.

Iterative Magnitude Pruning, and in particular IMP with local thresholds, consistently outperforms one-shot magnitude pruning across MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets.

The performance gap between Iterative Magnitude Pruning and one-shot magnitude pruning increases at sparsity levels above 70% across MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets.

At 80% sparsity, Iterative Magnitude Pruning with local (per-layer) thresholds (IMP-Local) yields a 1–2 percentage-point accuracy advantage over one-shot magnitude pruning on OpenForensic and up to a 2–3 percentage-point advantage on FaceForensics++ across MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet.
The iterative refinement in Iterative Magnitude Pruning better preserves subtle discriminative features needed for deepfake detection than one-shot magnitude pruning.
The effectiveness of global versus local pruning criteria in Iterative Magnitude Pruning is dataset-dependent.

In Iterative Magnitude Pruning, global pruning (using a single threshold based on all weights) generalizes better and is more stable than local pruning (using per-layer thresholds) on the cleaner, less compressed OpenForensic dataset (140,000 training images, no face cropping).

In Iterative Magnitude Pruning, local pruning (using per-layer thresholds) better preserves accuracy than global pruning (using a single threshold based on all weights) on the challenging, heavily compressed FaceForensics++ dataset (11,600 training images from 400 face-cropped videos with varied compression artifacts).

In Iterative Magnitude Pruning, dataset statistics and compression artifacts determine which pruning strategy best preserves manipulation-sensitive features: global pruning (using a single threshold based on all weights) versus local pruning (using per-layer thresholds).
Pruned subnetworks maintain concentrated attention on semantically meaningful facial regions even at 80% sparsity.
The attention maps of the pruned subnetworks contract and focus on smaller regions.
Pruned networks increasingly emphasize high-frequency artifacts and temporal inconsistencies over broader semantic features as sparsity increases.

Sparse subnetworks discovered via Iterative Magnitude Pruning on the larger OpenForensic dataset transfer effectively to the smaller FaceForensics++ dataset when evaluated directly with no fine-tuning.
At 60% sparsity, an IMP-pruned MesoNet achieves 61.2% accuracy on FaceForensics++, compared to its dense baseline accuracy on FaceForensics++ of 59.9%.
At 80% sparsity, an IMP-pruned CNN-5 subnetwork achieves 74.5% accuracy (dense baseline on FaceForensics++: 76.2%)
an IMP-pruned ResNet-18 subnetwork achieves 83.7% accuracy (dense baseline: 85.3%).

When evaluated directly with no fine-tuning, sparse subnetworks discovered via Iterative Magnitude Pruning and found on a larger source dataset can be reused on a smaller target dataset with minor accuracy degradation or, in some cases, modest improvement compared to the dense baseline.

When pruned using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), larger, deeper architectures exhibit greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior than compact networks on both the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets.
Compact networks are more sensitive to pruning and degrade more quickly than larger, deeper architectures.
claim 23 and claim 24 establish an architecture-dependent trade-off between base model compactness and compressibility.
Under Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), starting with a larger model yields subnetworks that are both small and robust.
Very compact models may lack sufficient redundancy to tolerate extreme pruning.

In cross-dataset transfer experiments, subnetworks produced by Iterative Magnitude Pruning consistently outperform one-shot-pruned subnetworks at both 60% and 80% sparsity across MesoNet, CNN-5, and ResNet-18.
Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) produces subnetworks with superior generalization across datasets, as claim 28 shows.
Pruned subnetworks maintain concentrated attention on the cheek and eye areas even at 80% sparsity.

When pruned using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), ResNet-18 (11.7M parameters) exhibits greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior than compact networks on both the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets.
MesoNet (0.015M parameters) is more sensitive to pruning and degrades more quickly than larger, deeper architectures.

In the zero-shot cross-dataset transfer experiments from OpenForensic to FaceForensics++, subnetworks produced by Iterative Magnitude Pruning consistently outperform one-shot-pruned subnetworks at both 60% and 80% sparsity across MesoNet, CNN-5, and ResNet-18.

note.text: elaboration of claim 15, claim 16: The attention difference is quantified via the Frobenius norm $\Delta L^c(p)=\| L_{\text{original}}^c - L_p^c \|_F$, where $L_{\text{original}}^c$ is the Grad-CAM heatmap for class $c$ from the original dense model and $L_p^c$ is the heatmap from the model at pruning rate $p$.
